idiom_name: content: @Composable (State) -> Unit parameter on the owning composable
implementation_notes: Kotlin makes the render function an ordinary function-typed parameter - the language docs call functions first-class values that 'can be passed as arguments to and returned from other higher-order functions' - and Jetpack Compose specialises that into the slot API: a composable takes content: @Composable (State) -> Unit (or a lambda with receiver) and invokes it in its own layout, so the caller supplies the UI while the composable owns the state. The classic component structure is replaced by this parameter; state hoisting plus a content lambda is the ordinary Compose shape, and CompositionLocal covers the cases where threading the lambda through every level is impractical. In Android Views the same decision is the adapter's onCreateViewHolder/onBindViewHolder pair, where the caller-supplied adapter creates and binds each item's views.
pitfalls: A composable lambda that reads the owner's state in the parent's scope recomposes the wrong range; pass the values the content needs as parameters so recomposition stays scoped to the call site.
Lambda parameters participate in Compose's skipping rules: an unstable or recreated lambda forces recomposition, so make callbacks stable (remember, method references) where profiling shows cost.
Heavy work inside the content lambda runs on every recomposition of the owner, not once per state change.

variants.name: Android Views adapter (RecyclerView.Adapter)
variants.implementation_notes: Before Compose, Android's rendering seam was the adapter: the API reference describes it as the binding from an app-specific data set to the views displayed in a RecyclerView, with onCreateViewHolder creating the view hierarchy and onBindViewHolder called by RecyclerView to display the data at the specified position. The caller-supplied adapter therefore owns every visual decision while the RecyclerView owns recycling, layout and lifecycle - the same inversion expressed as an object interface instead of a lambda. Keep it for view-based screens and older Android render paths; prefer the Compose content lambda for new declarative UI, whose slot parameter is the closer analogue of a render prop.
pitfalls: Holders are recycled, so onBindViewHolder must be idempotent and must not allocate view state per call; listeners bound there can leak references to recycled items.
Mutating the backing list or calling notifyDataSetChanged from inside a bind desynchronizes the adapter from the layout pass - the API requires the notifyItem* methods.
An adapter is not a view-model: state kept only in the adapter is lost on configuration change unless it is hoisted.
